Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976) was a high-ranking officer in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). He was born and raised in Tasmania and enlisted in the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934. Prior to World War II, he focused on flying instruction and navigation. In April 1941, he took command of No. 2 Squadron, which operated Lockheed Hudson aircraft. The squadron was sent to Dutch Timor in December, where it engaged Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. After returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam served in various staff roles and training commands, concluding the war with the rank of group captain.

In 1946, Headlam held the position of Officer Commanding North Western Area, and from 1947 to 1950, he served as the Director of Training. During the Malayan Emergency in 1950-51, he was stationed in Singapore, commanding No. 90 (Composite) Wing and later RAF Tengah. He acted as Air Member for Personnel on two occasions, in 1957 and from 1959 to 1960, and was honored with the title Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. After being promoted to air vice marshal, he went on to occupy the roles of Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command from 1961 to 1962, AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff from 1965 to 1966, and AOC Support Command from 1966 to 1967. In 1965, he was made a Companion of the Order of the Bath. After serving as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam, the son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam, was born on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania. He attended <unk> College in Hobart and completed his matriculation in 1932. Defying his parents' wishes, he enlisted in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. He received flying training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) at RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and was commissioned as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

After finishing a conversion course, Headlam was assigned to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. As noted in the official history of the pre-war RAAF, the Seaplane Squadron was no larger than a flight and was a component of No. 1 FTS, operating Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes, among other aircraft. During this assignment, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on 1 July 1935 and authored a paper on national defense, in which he proposed that with "strong air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses, Australia may be made practically invulnerable." Air Force historian Alan Stephens remarked that this paper "effectively defined the 'anti-lodgment' concept, which has been a consistent aspect of RAAF strategic thought."

In July 1936, Headlam completed a flying instructors course and subsequently joined the staff at No. 1 FTS. He was promoted to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Beginning in July 1938, he participated as one of six students in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, conducted by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This course featured several remarkable training flights that garnered significant media coverage, including a twelve-day, 10,800-kilometre (6,700 mi) circumnavigation of Australia in November, with Headlam piloting one of three Avro Ansons. In the following month, he commanded the three Ansons on a six-day round trip over Central Australia. He later excelled in the navigation course, earning special distinction. On January 27, 1939, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander. Initially, he served with No. 2 Squadron before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on August 29, with both squadrons operating Ansons.

After the onset of World War II, No. 1 Squadron was involved in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance operations off the southeastern coast of Australia. Headlam continued his role as a flight commander within the squadron until January 15, 1940, when he was transferred to Headquarters Laverton to serve as the station navigation officer. On March 27, he was assigned to the staff at RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He achieved the rank of squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Just two weeks later, he wed Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston, and the couple would later welcome a son and a daughter.

On 15 April 1941, Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton and was promoted to wing commander on 1 July. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily carried out maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December, when four of its aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, due to concerns over potential Japanese aggression in the Pacific. On 7 December, this group set up operations at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons of No. 2 Squadron remained on standby in Darwin. The next day, now aware that Australia was at war in the Pacific, one of the Hudsons based at Penfui attacked the Japanese vessel Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio ship, and successfully forced it aground. By 12 December, Headlam had moved to Penfui, taking on the role of commanding officer for both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, the aircraft of No. 2 Squadron were stationed at Penfui, <unk> Island, and Darwin. The unit at Penfui launched attacks on Japanese shipping involved in the Celebes invasion. On January 11, two Hudsons engaged and either shot down or damaged three Japanese floatplanes that were assaulting them while they bombed a transport ship; however, the following day, both Hudsons were shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros. Penfui was bombed by the Japanese for the first time on January 26, 1942, and subsequent regular attacks caused damage to several aircraft. The undamaged Hudsons were relocated to Darwin, but Headlam and his team stayed at Penfui to allow the base to support reconnaissance flights from Australia. On February 18, Headlam received orders to evacuate all personnel except a small team to help demolish the airfield with support from Sparrow Force. He returned to Darwin the next day, coinciding with the city's first Japanese air raid. In that attack, four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons were destroyed, while the rest were moved to Daly Waters, where they continued reconnaissance and bombing operations against Japanese positions in Timor.

Headlam continued his role in Darwin as the Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command until May 12, 1942, when he was transferred to Nhill, Victoria, to serve as the commanding officer of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which operated Ansons. In June, the personnel from the school established No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron. On July 20, 1943, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School ( <unk> ), also flying Ansons, located in Mount Gambier, South Australia. He was promoted to group captain on December 1, 1943, and on December 9, he became the first commanding officer of No. 3 <unk>, which operated Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. After he transferred command of No. 3 <unk>, he began his studies at RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. He was appointed the senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command on January 12, 1945.

In January 1946, Headlam was appointed Officer Commanding North Western Area. At the end of that year, he was assigned to Britain, where he attended the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and worked with the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon his return to Australia in November 1947, he took on the role of Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, he succeeded Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as the commander of No. 90 (Composite) Wing, which was based at RAF Changi in Singapore. No. 90 Wing oversaw RAAF units operating during the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, which flew Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, operating Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns carried out area bombing missions over areas controlled by communists and targeted specific locations, while the Dakotas were responsible for courier flights, VIP transport, and medical evacuations throughout Southeast Asia, as well as airlifting troops and supplies and dropping propaganda leaflets in Malaya. On December 20, Headlam sustained minor injuries when a Dakota from No. 38 Squadron, which he was co-piloting during a supply drop, crash-landed at Kampong Aur in Pahang due to engine failure. In August 1951, he was appointed commander of RAF Tengah in Singapore while continuing his role as commanding officer of No. 90 Wing. He transferred command of No. 90 Wing in December 1951.

On February 19, 1952, Headlam took on the role of senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales. During his tenure as SASO, the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) began to re-equip with English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. The Air Force also experienced a significant organizational shift, moving from a command-and-control structure based on geography to one based on function. This change led to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. Eastern Area Command, regarded as a de facto operational headquarters due to the number of combat units it oversaw, was restructured into Home Command in October 1953. In recognition of his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty," Headlam was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours. He was promoted to acting air commodore in May, and on October 7, 1954, his appointment as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced.

On 1 January 1955, Headlam was elevated to the rank of substantive air commodore. In November of that year, he was assigned to the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and the following year he pursued studies at the Imperial Defence College. Upon his return to Australia, he served as the acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra from 19 March to 21 October 1957, filling the role between Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters, and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960, between Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. In this capacity, Headlam was a member of the Air Board, which is the governing body of the service made up of its senior officers and led by the Chief of the Air Staff. He also served as one of two RAAF representatives on a committee chaired by businessman William John Allison that reviewed defense service conditions; the committee's recommendations resulted in a significant increase in flight pay, among other enhancements. Headlam held additional roles at the Department of Air, including Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, the latter of which put him in charge of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. In the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours, published on 3 June, he was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE). In May 1960, he took on the role of acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam became part of the Operational Command (OPCOM) team, which was the successor to Home Command and was tasked with overseeing RAAF operational units. In April, he succeeded Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as the Air Officer Commanding (AOC) of OPCOM. He was elevated to the rank of air vice marshal on May 29. On July 17, 1962, he was assigned to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya, and just a week later, he assumed the role of AOC for No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch replaced him as AOC OPCOM. During his tenure as AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam was in charge of regional air defense and offensive air operations amid the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 and the ensuing Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially started the following month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on January 20, 1964. He transferred command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris on November 30.

Upon returning to Australia, Headlam took on the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on 26 January 1965. He was honored as a Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on 22 June for his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories." His time as DCAS coincided with the most extensive rearmament initiative the Air Force had pursued since World War II, which was accompanied by manpower shortages resulting from this expansion and Australia’s growing commitment to security in Southeast Asia. Towards the end of his term, the first RAAF helicopters were deployed to the Vietnam War, and in March 1966, he traveled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff, Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, to strategize their deployment. A year prior, Wilton had suggested to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, that two Iroquois helicopters be sent to Vietnam for familiarization; however, Murdoch declined the request, leaving the RAAF helicopter squadron inadequately prepared for its cooperative role with the army upon deployment. On 8 August 1966, Headlam succeeded Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as Air Officer Commanding Support Command in Melbourne, which had been established in 1959 through the merger of the RAAF’s former Training and Maintenance Commands. On 1 January 1968, he was assigned to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff. Additionally, he served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971.

Upon his return to Australia in June 1971, Headlam took a period of resettlement leave prior to his retirement from the Air Force on August 3. He settled in Melbourne, where he passed away at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, following a long fight against cancer. He is survived by his children and his second wife. A private funeral was held for him, and he was cremated at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a state trunkline located in the Lower Peninsula of Michigan, USA, connecting Fremont and Howard City. The stretch between Newaygo and Howard City passes through Fremont and runs along the southern border of the Manistee National Forest. This rendition of M-82 is actually the state's second iteration; the original appeared in the Upper Peninsula around 1919. The routing in the Lower Peninsula has been in place since the 1920s. Over the years, various extensions and reductions have moved the endpoint as far west as New Era or Hesperia. The current alignment was established in the late 1970s.

M @-@ 82 starts at a junction with M @-@ 120 and B @-@ 96, located west of Fremont. This junction marks the convergence of three county lines. M @-@ 120 serves as the north-south boundary between Newaygo and Oceana, as well as Newaygo and Muskegon counties. B @-@ 96 establishes the east-west boundary for Oceana and Muskegon counties, running directly west of the intersection. M @-@ 82 departs the intersection heading east. The highway travels along 48th Street through agricultural areas until it reaches the community of Fremont. Once in town, it becomes Main Street, passing through the downtown area before M @-@ 82 turns south onto Stewart Avenue as it exits the city. The highway then curves and shifts to 72nd Street, continuing east through additional farmland. As M @-@ 82 approaches Newaygo, the landscape becomes increasingly wooded near the Muskegon River. The route follows Fremont Street eastward to where it intersects with M @-@ 37. The two highways merge, continuing together across the river and into downtown along State Street. Just south of downtown, M @-@ 82 veers east again, separating from M @-@ 37, and runs along 82nd Street at the southern border of the Manistee National Forest. The eastern terminus of M @-@ 82 is located at exit 118 on US 131 / M @-@ 46, west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT), in fulfilling its maintenance duties, monitors the traffic volume on its roadways. This traffic volume is quantified using a metric known as average annual daily traffic (AADT), which represents the traffic count for a specific road segment on an average day throughout the year. In 2009, MDOT's data revealed that a stretch of M-82 west of Fremont experienced the highest traffic volume for the highway, with 16,532 vehicles per day. Conversely, the lowest traffic count recorded was 4,018 vehicles east of Newaygo. Furthermore, MDOT has not designated any part of the highway as part of the National Highway System, which comprises roads significant to the nation’s economy, defense, and transportation.

The current M-82 was established in 1926. It extended from US 31 in Hart to the northern intersection of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. The highway traversed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, taking over the route of M-41. In late 1936, M-46 was extended along the section connecting Newaygo to Howard City, creating a concurrency between M-46 and M-82 to complete a gap in the M-46 path. By 1938, this concurrent segment became solely M-46, which reduced M-82 back to the northern junction with M-37 in Newaygo. In late 1947 or early 1948, the highway was realigned to a new route west of Ferry, changing its direction from northwest toward Hart to a westward end in Shelby.

In 1963 and 1964, the western end of the highway underwent two realignments. This adjustment rerouted it to extend from Hesperia to New Era, bypassing Ferry. A significant alteration around 1969 modified the highway designations in Oceana County. M-20 replaced M-82 west of Hesperia, terminating at New Era instead of Muskegon. The designation M-120 took over M-20 south of Hesperia, while M-82 was now limited to a route from Hesperia to Newaygo. In 1973, the length of the highway was extended when the eastern terminus was relocated back to Howard City. M-46 was redirected to align with the US 131 freeway south of Howard City to Cedar Springs, replacing M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This adjustment allowed the highway from Newaygo to Howard City to revert to the M-82 designation. The final modification occurred in 1978 when the overlap with M-120 was removed, favoring M-120 instead. At this point, the M-82 designation was shortened to the junction west of Fremont, resulting in the current routing of the highway.

Meridian ranks as the sixth largest city in Mississippi, USA. It serves as the county seat for Lauderdale County and is the main city in the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. The city is located along key highways, positioned 93 miles (150 kilometers) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 kilometers) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Founded in 1860 at the junction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian's economy was developed around the railroads and the goods they carried, establishing it as a key trading hub. In February 1864, during the American Civil War, General William Tecumseh Sherman set fire to a significant portion of the city during the Battle of Meridian.

After the war, the city was reconstructed and entered what is known as a "Golden Age," becoming the largest city in Mississippi from 1890 to 1930 and emerging as a major manufacturing hub in the South, with 44 trains arriving and departing each day. Union Station, established in 1906, now serves as a multi-modal hub, providing access to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, with an average of 242,360 passengers annually. Although the economy experienced a downturn with the decline of the railroad sector, the city successfully diversified, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors employing the majority of workers by 2010. The estimated population within the city limits, based on 2008 census data, is 38,232, while the broader population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius is 232,900, and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, with 104,600 and 234,200 individuals respectively participating in the labor force, contributing to the city's economy.

The region is supported by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which collectively offer more than 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and is also the first local Department of Homeland Security established in the state. Key Field is named in honor of brothers Fred and Al Key, who set a world endurance flight record in 1935. Currently, the field accommodates the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and acts as a support facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Additionally, Rush Foundation Hospital stands as the largest non-military employer in the area, providing jobs for 2,610 individuals.

Within the city's diverse array of arts institutions and historic structures are the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Meridian hosted two Carnegie libraries, designated for white and African American communities. The Carnegie Branch Library, which has since been torn down, was among several Carnegie libraries constructed for African Americans in the Southern United States during the period of segregation.

The city has been chosen as the future site for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center ( <unk> ). Jimmie Rodgers, known as the "Father of Country Music," was born in Meridian. Within Highland Park, there is a museum that showcases memorabilia from his life and career, alongside railroad artifacts from the steam engine era. The park also features the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, recognized as a National Historic Landmark, and it is the only existing two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie in the world. Other notable individuals from the area include Susan Akin, Miss America 1986, James Chaney, an activist who was murdered during the Mississippi civil rights movement in 1964, and Hartley Peavey, the founder of Peavey Electronics, which is based in Meridian. The federal courthouse hosted the trial from 1966 to 1967 for those accused in the murders of Chaney and two other activists; this marked the first instance in which a white jury convicted a white official for a civil rights-related murder.

The region now known as Meridian was once home to the Choctaw Native Americans and was acquired by the United States through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830, amidst the era of Indian Removal. Following the ratification of the treaty, European American settlers began to migrate into the area.

After obtaining a federal land grant of approximately 2,000 acres (810 hectares), Richard McLemore, the inaugural settler of Meridian, started to offer free land to newcomers in an effort to attract more settlers and foster growth in the area. In 1853, most of McLemore's land was purchased by Lewis A. Ragsdale, an attorney from Alabama. The remaining 80 acres (0.32 km²) were acquired by John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County. Recognized as the city's founders, Ragsdale and Ball commenced the process of dividing their respective parcels into lots for future development.

There was significant rivalry regarding the name chosen for the settlement. Ball, along with the city's more industrial inhabitants, favored the name "Meridian," considering it synonymous with "junction." In contrast, the more agrarian residents preferred "<unk>" (which translates to "mad river" in a Native American language), named after a nearby creek. Ragsdale suggested "Ragsdale City." Ball constructed a station house on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, with a sign that alternated daily between "Meridian" and "<unk>." Ultimately, the ongoing expansion of the railroads led to an influx of railroad workers, who prevailed over the other residents and established "Meridian" as the permanent name on the station. The town was officially incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

At the onset of the American Civil War in 1861, Meridian was a modest village. Its advantageous location at a railroad junction prompted the Confederates to establish several military facilities to aid their efforts in the conflict. During the Battle of Meridian in 1864, General William Tecumseh Sherman led his forces into the town, obliterating the railroads in all directions and demolishing an arsenal and large warehouses; much of the town's infrastructure was set ablaze. Sherman allegedly remarked afterward, "Meridian, with its depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments no longer exists." Nonetheless, the railroad lines within the city were quickly restored and resumed operations just 26 working days after the battle. During the Reconstruction period, race relations remained strained, exemplified by the riot of 1871 that erupted following a fire damaging numerous businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town experienced significant growth and entered its "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910. The presence of railroads in the region facilitated transportation and attracted various industries, leading to a surge in population. As the number of residents increased, so did commercial activities in the downtown area. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian became the largest city in Mississippi and emerged as a prominent manufacturing hub in the South. Many of the city’s notable historic structures were constructed during this period and shortly thereafter, including the Grand Opera House in 1890, the Wechsler School in 1894, two Carnegie libraries in 1913, and the <unk> Building, which became Meridian's tallest skyscraper in 1929.

The city experienced continued growth due to the efforts of a commission government that aimed to establish 90 new industrial plants in 1913, along with a thriving automobile sector in the 1920s. Even in the face of the 1929 stock market crash and the subsequent Great Depression, the city managed to draw in new businesses. As escapism became a cultural trend during the depths of the Depression, the S. H. Kress & Co. building, designed to "offer luxury to the common man," opened in downtown Meridian, alongside the Temple Theater, which served as a cinema. Additionally, the federal courthouse was constructed in 1933 as part of a WPA initiative.

Following a short period of economic slowdown at the conclusion of the Depression, the nation entered World War II, which revitalized the significance of railroads. The railways were crucial for transporting gasoline and scrap metal for military vehicle production, leading to Meridian's resurgence as the area's rail hub. This renewed economic growth persisted until the 1950s, when automobiles and the Interstate Highway System gained greater popularity over passenger trains. The railroad industry's downturn led to substantial job losses, prompting a population decrease as workers migrated to other regions.

During the 1960s American Civil Rights Movement, Meridian housed an office for the Council of Federated Organizations (CFO) along with various other activist groups. Local residents like James Chaney, alongside Michael <unk>, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman—volunteers from the North—worked to establish a community center that offered classes aimed at empowering African Americans in the region to reclaim their voting rights. This activism sparked resentment among local whites, often escalating into violence due to heightened racial tensions. In June 1964, Chaney, <unk>, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to speak with members of a black church that had suffered from a bombing and arson. That night, the three vanished while returning to Meridian. After an extensive FBI investigation, their bodies were discovered two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

Seven members of the Ku Klux Klan, including a deputy sheriff, were found guilty in the federal courthouse in Meridian of "depriving the victims of their civil rights," while three others were acquitted during the trial concerning the murders of civil rights workers in Mississippi. This marked the first instance of a white jury convicting "a white official in a civil rights homicide." In 2005, the state reopened the case, leading to charges being filed for the first time. Edgar Ray Killen was convicted of manslaughter and received a 60-year prison sentence. In honor of Chaney, Meridian later renamed a section of 49th Avenue after him and began holding an annual memorial service.

Beginning in the 1960s, with the development of highways that facilitated commuting, residents started relocating from downtown to newly established housing subdivisions in the north. As strip commercial developments began to encroach on the downtown area, the city took steps in the 1970s and 80s to identify multiple zones as historic districts in order to maintain the city's architectural integrity. In 1979, the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was established, followed by the founding of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street initiated multiple projects aimed at revitalizing downtown, which included the establishment of a new Amtrak Station in 1997, inspired by the design of the historic train station that once served the city during its Golden Age before being demolished. Additional efforts encompassed the renovation of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, along with promoting integrated urban design. In collaboration with The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street also played a key role in the renovation and adaptation of the historic Grand Opera House in 2006, transforming it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

Following the transfer of ownership of Meridian Main Street to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in late 2007, both organizations, along with the Meridian Downtown Association, led the initiative for downtown revitalization. The Alliance acts as an overarching entity, providing support staff and resources to the other two groups, while also serving as a communication link among them. Plans were in motion to renovate the <unk> Building; however, newly elected Mayor Cheri Barry halted those plans in early 2010. Currently, the Alliance is focused on encouraging further development and restoration in the downtown area, aiming to support businesses like specialty shops, restaurants, and bars which contribute to a vibrant atmosphere both day and night. Meanwhile, the Meridian Downtown Association is dedicated to boosting foot traffic in the downtown area by organizing special events, while the Meridian Main Street program is focused on supporting the existing businesses in the vicinity.

Due to Meridian's position as a railway junction, the area has seen the establishment of numerous hotels to accommodate its travelers. Even prior to Meridian's "Golden Age," several significant hotels, such as the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue hotels, were constructed before the 20th century began. As the railroads expanded and the original Union Station was built in 1906, additional hotels were erected for the convenience of passengers and workers. The Elmira Hotel was built in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian opened its doors in 1907, while Union Hotel was established in 1908. In 1979, Union Hotel was added to the National Register of Historic Places, and both Hotel Meridian and Grand Avenue Hotel were recognized as contributing properties to the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

As the city expanded, the hotels mirrored the aspirations of a robust economy, exemplified by the Lamar Hotel, an eleven-story skyscraper erected in 1927. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and later repurposed as a county annex building. In 1988, it earned recognition as a Mississippi Landmark.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel became a cornerstone in the African American business district that emerged to the west of the city's center. During the era of segregation, it was one of the few establishments in the city where traveling African Americans could secure accommodations.

During the 1960s and '70s, the expansion of city suburbs led to a significant number of hotels relocating from downtown areas. The renovation of the Riley Center in 2006 heightened the demand for a new hotel in the downtown region. A proposal was made to redevelop the <unk> Building for this initiative; however, efforts to restore it were hindered by a shift in city leadership. In 2013, the <unk> Preservation Society was established to promote public awareness and backing for the building's restoration, which included first-floor tours and anniversary celebrations.

The Meridian Downtown Historic District combines two previous districts: the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. Since 1985, Meridian has functioned under a mayor-council or "strong mayor" system of governance. The mayor is elected by the entire population every four years. Additionally, five city council members are elected every four years, with each representing one of the five wards, which are regarded as single-member districts. As the city’s chief executive officer, the mayor oversees and directs the daily operations of the city government. Meanwhile, the city council acts as the legislative branch, responsible for establishing policies and approving the city’s operating budget each year.

City Hall, recognized on the National Register of Historic Places, is situated at 601 23rd Avenue. The mayor currently serving is Percy Bland. The city council comprises Dr. George M. Thomas from Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon from Ward 5. Pam McInnis holds the position of council clerk. Overall, the city has a workforce of 570 employees.

Following Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city created a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), making it the sole local DHS in the state. This team manages an area encompassing nine counties. After receiving $2.5 million in grants from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and various organizations, the department initiated training for law enforcement officers from other Southern states in passenger rail rescue, while also providing civilian courses in basic handgun use, Boy Scout first aid, hunting, and firearms training. The DHS plays a crucial role during emergencies, as seen during Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, when it assisted in establishing and supporting shelters for 700 evacuees. Currently, the city leads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which is a collaboration of three teams covering nine counties each.

Led by Police Chief Lee <unk> since 2009, the Meridian Police Department comprises 115 full-time officers along with part-time and reserve personnel. In 2009, the department's Criminal Investigations Division handled 4,000 cases, with 2,000 classified as felonies. In 2009, <unk> crimes were reported, showing a slight increase from the previous year’s figures. Meridian is regarded as "the safest city in Mississippi with a population exceeding 30,000." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, situated in unincorporated Lauderdale County near Meridian, is managed by the GEO Group for the Mississippi Department of Corrections. Anthony Clayton serves as the chief of the Meridian Fire Department, which responded to over 1,600 calls in 2009, including 123 structural fires and 609 emergency service requests.

Before this transition to the Republican Party, white voters in the area backed candidates from the Democratic Party, as the region was dominated by a single party for many decades following the late nineteenth century.

The city's expansion has mirrored the influence of various social and economic dynamics. From its establishment until 1970, the total population rose with each census, although the growth rates fluctuated significantly, ranging from as high as 165% to as low as 0.2%. In the 1970 census, the population saw a decrease, followed by a slight increase by 1980, after which it gradually declined until the beginning of the 21st century when it began to rise again. Between 1980 and 2000, the population decreased by over 14%. According to the 2000 census, the city's population stood at 39,968, with a population density of 885.9 inhabitants per square mile (342.0/km²). By 2008, the city ranked as the sixth largest in the state, and there was a population increase noted in 2010.

Meridian serves as the central city in the Meridian area, which, as of 2009, included three counties: Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale, with a population of 106,139. Within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, the population totals 232,900, and within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, it reaches 526,500.

Although the city's total population growth has fluctuated, there has been a consistent increase in both the number and proportion of non-white residents. The only decrease within this demographic occurred from 1960 to 1970, coinciding with a significant drop in the city’s overall population. According to the 2010 Census, the racial composition of the city included 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.09% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% from two or more races. Individuals identifying as Hispanic or Latino of any race constituted 1.75% of the population.

As per the 2000 Census, there were 17,890 housing units within city limits, with 15,966 being occupied, and 10,033 of these homes were occupied by families. Among the occupied households, 31.1% had children under 18 years, 36.2% were married couples living together, 23.3% were headed by a female householder without a husband present, and 37.2% were non-family households. Individuals made up 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% included someone living alone aged 65 or older. The average household size was 2.39, while the average family size was 3.06. Since 1970, the average household size has consistently declined from 3.04. Additionally, Meridian's median age rose from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

The median household income in the city was $25,085, while the median income for families was $31,062. Males earned a median income of $29,404, compared to $19,702 for females. The city's per capita income stood at $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the overall population lived below the poverty line, which included 40.8% of individuals under 18 years old and 22.0% of those aged 65 and older.

The population of Meridian and the surrounding areas is quite religiously active, with 65.2% of Lauderdale County residents identifying as members of a religious congregation, in contrast to the national average of 50.2%. In the year 2000, among those affiliated, 30,068 individuals (59.0%) were part of the Southern Baptist Convention, 9,469 (18.6%) belonged to the United Methodist Church, and 1,872 (3.7%) were connected to the Catholic Church.

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe played a significant role in the commercial growth of the city, establishing various businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, right before the city's "Golden Age." In 1927, Meridian boasted the largest Jewish community in the state, with 575 Jewish residents. Currently, there are fewer than 40 Jews residing in Meridian, the majority of whom are elderly.

Meridian is situated in the North Central Hills area of Mississippi within Lauderdale County. As reported by the United States Census Bureau, the city encompasses a total area of 45.9 square miles (119 km²), of which 45.1 square miles (117 km²) is land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) is water. In terms of major highways, Meridian is positioned 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The region surrounding the city features cotton and corn fields, alongside oak and pine forests, with its landscape characterized by clay hills and the lowlands near the headwaters of the unnamed river.

The city's urban core has undergone alterations to its natural landscape through grading, yet the surrounding areas retain their gently rolling topography. The city is dotted with numerous small creeks, while small lakes and woodlands are located in both the northern and southern regions. <unk> Creek traverses the southern area and divides into Gallagher's Creek, which flows through the city's center. Loper's Creek is situated in the extreme western part of the city, and several smaller creeks, such as Shearer’s Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek, are scattered across the city.

Meridian falls within the humid subtropical climate zone. During the summer months (June to August), the average high temperature hovers around 90 °F (32 °C), while the average low is approximately 70 °F (21 °C). In the winter months (December to February), the average maximum temperature is about 60 °F (16 °C), with an average minimum of 35 °F (2 °C). July is the hottest month, featuring an average high of 92.9 °F (33.8 °C), whereas January is the coldest month, recording an average low of 34.7 °F (1.5 °C).

The city's average annual precipitation is 58.65 inches (1,490 mm). Rainfall is relatively consistent over the year, with March being the wettest month, receiving an average of 6.93 inches (176 mm) of rain. A significant portion of the rainfall comes from thunderstorms, which are prevalent in the summer but can happen at any time of the year. Severe thunderstorms, capable of causing damaging winds and large hail, along with the usual dangers of lightning and heavy rainfall, can occur. These severe events are most frequent in the spring and have a secondary occurrence peak in the fall. Additionally, these storms carry the potential for tornadoes.

In its early days, the economy heavily relied on the railroads in the region. By the early 20th century, the city had become the largest in Mississippi, featuring five major rail lines and 44 trains arriving and departing each day. The local economy was not only tied to the railroads but also to the goods transported via them, including timber and cotton. Between approximately 1890 and 1930, these rail-related industries made the city a significant economic force within the state and the surrounding area. Although the economy experienced a downturn with the decline of the railroad industry in the 1950s, the city has successfully adapted, transitioning from a primarily railroad-based economy to a more diversified one, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing now providing the majority of employment.

In addition to Lauderdale County and the city of Marion, Meridian is supported by the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, established in 1996 by local business leaders. As of April 2010, the city had a civilian labor force of just 15,420 individuals, while the population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius stands at 232,900, and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, with labor force figures of 104,600 and 234,200 respectively. Consequently, the city acts as a center for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural activities. Eighty percent of the workforce in Lauderdale County lives within the county, and 90% reside within 45 miles.

As of April 2010, Lauderdale County had a total of 6,260 individuals working in the healthcare sector. The largest healthcare institution in the area is Rush Hospital, which employs 2,610 people, followed by East Mississippi State Hospital with 1,500 employees, and Anderson Hospital with 1,475 staff members. Meridian is home to three hospitals and various other healthcare-related facilities. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers services such as cardiovascular surgery, a Level II newborn intensive care unit, and a health and fitness center. Additionally, Rush Foundation Hospital and its affiliate, Rush Health Systems, run the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, which provides long-term care for patients needing extended recovery in a hospital environment. Riley Hospital features two centers dedicated to stroke treatment and rehabilitation services. Other healthcare establishments in Meridian include the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, which has been operational since 1882.

Retail serves as a significant source of employment in the county, with 5,280 individuals working in this sector as of April 2010. The city sees nearly $2 billion spent on retail purchases each year. The Bonita Lakes Mall, covering 633,685 square feet (58,871 m²), features over a hundred shopping options, such as department stores, specialty shops, dining establishments, and United Artists Theatres. The first phase of the Meridian Crossroads shopping center, which spans 375,000 square feet (34,800 m²) in the Bonita Lakes area, was completed in November 2007, significantly enhancing the local retail landscape. Additionally, the shopping district on North Hills Street has been growing, with new retail and office spaces opening in March 2007 near the Walmart Supercenter on Highway 19.

The region is supported by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which provide over 4,000 jobs for local residents. NAS Meridian is responsible for training naval carrier pilots and other enlisted members. Additionally, it hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCDTA), which offers narcotics training for law enforcement agencies across several southeastern states. The city boasts the first local Department of Homeland Security in the state and serves as the leader of a nine-county regional response team and a twenty-nine county regional response task force. Key Field is notable for the historic flight by brothers Fred and Al Key, who set a world endurance flight record in 1935. Currently, Key Field is home to the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and a support facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. The location also features an exhibit that highlights the history of aviation and houses Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County had a total of 2,850 individuals employed in manufacturing. Peavey Electronics Corporation, which has been producing guitars, amplifiers, and sound equipment since 1965, is headquartered in the city. Additional companies in the region consist of Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation. The city also features four industrial parks.

In the heart of downtown, the MSU Riley Center generates income through tourism, as well as arts and entertainment sales. Each year, the Riley Center draws over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian for various conferences, meetings, and performances. Loeb's Department Store, located on Front St, has stood as a clothing institution in Mississippi, enduring four generations of family ownership. Since its establishment by Alex Loeb in 1887, the store has offered high-quality apparel for both men and women.

With a rich history spanning over a century in the arts, Meridian is home to numerous cultural organizations and a variety of cultural events. Among the earliest art organizations in the city, The Meridian Art League was founded in February 1933. Initially, art exhibitions took place at the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian, but after rebranding to the Meridian Art Association in 1949, exhibitions were organized in different venues throughout the city. Following the closure of the Carnegie Library located at 25th Ave and 7th St, the Art Association transformed the site into the Meridian Museum of Art, providing a permanent venue for its exhibits. The museum opened its doors in 1970 and has since offered rotating exhibitions alongside numerous educational programs for both adults and students. Annually, over thirty exhibitions are hosted, showcasing a diverse range of works from traditional decorative arts to ethnographic and tribal materials, photography, crafts, and more. The museum's collection also features 18th and 19th-century portraits, 20th-century photography, and various sculptures.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) was established in 1978 as the official arts organization for Meridian and Lauderdale County. MCA manages the Community Art Grants program, hosts the annual <unk> Festival, conducts various workshops, and organizes additional special events each year. The council collaborates with numerous arts organizations in both the city and county, including the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, recognized as one of the oldest subscription-based community theatres in the South, was constructed in 1932 and currently entertains over 22,000 guests each season, making it the most attended community theatre in Mississippi. The Meridian Symphony Orchestra (<unk>), which was founded in 1961, held its inaugural concert in 1962 and launched its first full season in 1963. In 1965, the <unk> featured its first international soloist, Elena <unk>, as a performer with the orchestra. The Orchestra has supported the Meridian Public School District in establishing its own orchestra and strings programs, alongside assisting in the creation of the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, who has been the conductor since 1991, currently leads the orchestra, which will commemorate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The Grand Opera House of the city was established in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg. Throughout its years of operation, the venue showcased numerous renowned artists and productions, starting with a performance of Johann Strauss II’s "The Gypsy Baron" by a German troupe. However, the opera house shut its doors in the late 1920s as a result of the Great Depression, remaining derelict for nearly seven decades. A $10 million grant from the Riley Foundation, established locally in 1998, initiated the restoration of the building in 2000, supplemented by an additional $15 million sourced from a mix of city, county, and federal funding. The renovation of the opera house was finalized in September 2006, rebranded as the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." The Riley Center features a 950-seat auditorium for live events, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 m²) of meeting space, drawing over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian each year for conferences, meetings, and performances.

Meridian is justifiably regarded as an architectural gem, being one of the most well-preserved cities from the early 20th century in the nation. Architecture students from across the U.S. and Canada frequently visit Meridian in groups as part of their studies, attracted by the many buildings designed by prominent architects. Among them is the only residence in the Southern U.S. created by the renowned Canadian architect Louis S. Curtiss, who is celebrated for pioneering the glass curtain wall skyscraper, located on Highland Park. Slayer's guitarist Jeff Hanneman composed "Angel of Death" after delving into literature about Nazi doctor Josef Mengele while on tour with the band. His investigations targeted specific groups, such as dwarfs and twins, and encompassed both physical and psychological assessments. The song "Angel of Death" references several of the tests he conducted, including surgeries done without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, endurance isolation, gassing, injections with deadly pathogens, sex reassignment surgeries, organ and limb removals, and <unk>.

"Joining forces, but it's only a matter of time before you tear yourselves apart," is a line from the penultimate verse that refers to the accusation that Mengele operated on twins, one of whom was deformed. It was claimed that "the hunchback was stitched to the other child, back to back, their wrists also connected." This assertion was initially made by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS officer Adolf Eichmann, dubbed the "architect of the Holocaust," where it was alleged that Mengele "connected their veins" and transformed them into Siamese twins. This claim gained broader recognition when Vera Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary The Search for Mengele, which has been referenced by various authors, including Gerald Posner, a noted expert on Mengele.

The lyrics of "Angel of Death" played a significant role in postponing the launch of Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood. The band was under contract with Def Jam Records, whose distributor, Columbia Records, declined to release the album over concerns regarding its lyrical themes and artwork, labeling the artwork as "too graphic." Ultimately, Reign in Blood was released by Geffen Records on October 7, 1986. Nevertheless, because of the surrounding controversy, the album was not included in Geffen Records' official release schedule.
